source: SPEC_Workbook_Full — First Meeting - Alignment tab; Command Center (Question Zero)

sections.title: What's actually driving it
sections.intro: You said this is hurting. One question each — the point is to find the cause, not to catalogue the symptom.

questions.text: Safety — what's actually driving it?
options: The paperwork and records don't keep up
Clients or auditors keep raising it

questions.text: People — what's actually driving it?
options: Can't hire the ones we need
Nobody's clear what their job actually is

questions.text: Earnings — what's actually driving it?
options: Margin is thinner than it should be
Numbers arrive too late to act on
I don't trust the numbers I get
Busy but the cash isn't there

questions.text: Compliance — what's actually driving it?
options: Tickets and licences expire without warning
Records exist but can't be produced

sections.title: Question Zero
sections.intro: Ask this before anything else. If leadership can't answer clearly, that itself is information.

questions.text: Why bring SPEC in now? What was the specific moment or number that made this worth doing?

sections.title: Organisational diagnostic
sections.intro: Put two questions to leadership, directly, before scoring a single person. The answer decides how SPEC gets applied here — reinforcing an existing strength, or protecting it while building something new.

questions.text: What does this organisation do well, today? (core competence, in leadership's own words)
What is the evidence this is true? (client feedback, retention, safety record, financials)
What does this organisation want to do well — Year 1 ambition?
Year 2 ambition?
Year 3 ambition?
Is the Year 1–3 ambition the SAME as the current core competence, or DIFFERENT?
If SAME: SPEC's job is to reinforce and scale what already works. What does that mean in practice?
If DIFFERENT: SPEC's job is to protect the existing strength while deliberately building the new capability. What does that mean in practice?

sections.review: Revisit annually, or whenever leadership signals a strategic shift.

questions.text: Is the business functioning well?
Are the financials functioning well?
If the financials are not functioning: are the numbers themselves bad, or are the people/systems reading and reporting the numbers the problem?

sections.title: 1. What success looks like
sections.intro: This conversation happens in week one, before operations start. It's not about problems or systems. It's about what success actually looks like, what confidence means to the business owner, and how clarity enables them to step back. Record genuine answers — not the polite version.

questions.text: If the business was running at its absolute best, what would be different about how you spend your time?
What does a typical week look like when you've genuinely stepped back and the business is running well without you in every decision?
When you imagine having more time back, what has to be true about the business for that to actually happen?

sections.title: 2. The commercial reality — cost and revenue base
sections.intro: Bringing in a General Manager is itself a strong, positive step. This part isn't about finding fault. It's about building an honest, shared baseline of the true cost and revenue picture, so every decision from here is made on solid ground rather than a guess.

questions.text: Walk me through how the current cost base is calculated — direct labour, materials, overheads. Is this fully loaded, or are there costs not being captured?
Are compliance costs (licensing, insurance, safety systems, training) properly reflected in job and quote pricing, or absorbed as general overhead nobody's really tracking?
Has pricing been adjusted for the true cost of running the business safely and compliantly — or is there a gap between what should be charged and what's currently being charged?
If we invest properly in safety and compliance this year, what's the expected impact on margin? Has that been modelled, or is it currently unknown?
Where do you think the biggest gap is between perceived profitability and actual profitability?

sections.title: Cost and revenue coverage checklist
sections.intro: Go through every line, not just the ones that come up naturally. Where understanding is partial or unknown is where the first 90 days of clarity work goes.
items: Direct labour cost (wages, on-costs, super, workers comp)
Safety investment (training, PPE, systems, incident cost)
Insurance (public liability, workers comp, professional indemnity)
Quoting / pricing methodology — is margin accurate on every job?
Tender / bid cost vs win rate

sections.title: A realistic timeline — set this expectation now
sections.intro: Getting true costs and true revenue fully understood typically takes 3–6 months, not weeks. Real results show between 3 and 6–12 months; the minimum viable term is six months.

questions.text: What would a realistic 30-day / 90-day / 6-month view of this look like to you — what should be clear by when?
Right now, how do you know the business is running well? What do you actually look at?
If you had clear monthly visibility on Safety, People, Earnings and Compliance, what would that change about how confident you feel stepping back?
What's the one indicator that, if it went wrong, you'd need to know immediately?
When you're not in the weeds, what are you actually worried about — what could go sideways without you seeing it?
Tell me about a previous leader where trust broke down — what actually happened, and what was the real issue underneath?
How often do you want a board-style conversation — weekly, fortnightly, monthly?
What should that conversation look like — length, format?
What belongs in that conversation, and what should never come up?

sections.title: 6. Systems in use
sections.intro: What the business actually runs on today, function by function. This tells us what can be connected to SPEC, what stays manual, and what the real data quality looks like before relying on it.

sections.title: 7. NPS baseline
sections.intro: NPS is the leading indicator for Earnings — it shows trouble before it hits revenue. If it's not tracked yet, a leader's honest gut estimate is still a useful starting baseline.

questions.text: Do you currently measure Net Promoter Score or client satisfaction in any formal way? If so, what's the current number?
If not tracked: based on your gut sense of client sentiment, what would you estimate it to be?

sections.title: 8. How we'll work together — what we're agreeing to
sections.text: Safety, People, Earnings and Compliance are scored monthly and visible to you at any time. That data drives our board conversation — not gut feel, not time spent in the office. If something is red or amber on the scorecard, that is what we discuss; everything else stays off the table. You step back from day-to-day operations; the GM runs the business; you monitor via the scorecard and our agreed cadence. If trust is ever in question, we name it directly and come back to this covenant. Success is measured by the business running well, visibly, without you needing to be in every decision.

sections.title: 9. Early warning signs — name these now
sections.intro: These are the three ways this arrangement typically breaks down. Naming them now means if one starts to happen it's recognised as the known pattern, not a personal conflict.

patterns.name: Focus drifts to time, not outcomes
patterns.sign: The conversation becomes about hours in the office, visibility or presence instead of what the scorecard shows.
patterns.fix: Return to the scorecard. If nothing is flagged red or amber, there is nothing to discuss.

patterns.name: Difficulty letting go of day-to-day control
patterns.sign: Questions cover ground that isn't on the scorecard; delegated decisions get revisited; the GM is asked to justify things that are working.
patterns.fix: Ask directly: is this something the scorecard is flagging, or is this a different concern?

patterns.name: The system becomes onerous instead of clarifying
patterns.sign: SPEC eats hours to maintain, is used to justify rather than inform, or grows beyond its purpose.
patterns.fix: Keep the monthly update to roughly 20 minutes. If it's taking longer, simplify the system.

sections.title: 11. Success and failure — the definition
sections.failure: Not the business struggling — struggle is normal and often necessary. Failure is the leader's response to real visibility turning into avoidance, control-reversion, or disengagement — breaking the mechanism that surfaced the truth before it had a chance to work.
sections.success: Sustaining all three guiding principles together, over time, without one being quietly sacrificed to protect another — make money, do it safely, be a company everyone is proud to work at, year in, year out.
